# **Architectural Synthesis of QMINIWASM: Ternary Stabilizer Execution and Quantum-Assisted Routing**

The paradigm of extreme-edge artificial intelligence necessitates a radical departure from traditional von Neumann computational models and standard floating-point arithmetic. The QMINIWASM architecture represents a convergence of 1.58-bit ternary quantization and hybrid quantum-classical computing, specifically designed to execute non-linear attention mechanisms and high-dimensional operations. By constraining neural network weights to the discrete ternary set ![][image1] 1, computational overhead is drastically reduced. This quantization strategy replaces power-intensive matrix multiplications with pure addition and subtraction, leveraging the BitLinear transformation to maintain performance parity with 16-bit floating-point baselines.3

Simultaneously, the integration of quantum-assisted routing introduces the ability to evaluate complex, high-dimensional probability distributions via quantum circuits. However, leveraging physical Quantum Processing Units (QPUs) for all operations incurs unacceptable network latency, decoherence risks, and error-correction overheads. The Gottesman-Knill theorem provides the foundational mathematical solution: any quantum circuit restricted to the Clifford group—composed of Hadamard (H), Phase (S), and Controlled-NOT (CNOT) gates—acting on computational basis states and measured in the Pauli basis, can be efficiently simulated on a classical computer in polynomial time.4

The primary architectural objective of the QMINIWASM project is to aggressively optimize the quantum compiler and dynamic router to maximize the use of Clifford group gates, mapping their classical simulation directly onto the ultra-efficient 1.58-bit ternary Arithmetic Logic Units (ALUs) of the WebAssembly (WASM) runtime. This effectively creates a zero-multiplier, highly parallelized classical simulator for stabilizer states at the edge. Physical QPU offloading is strictly reserved for the non-Clifford boundary—specifically, operations such as the T-gate (![][image2] rotation) or the CCZ (Controlled-Controlled-Z) gate, which elevate the Clifford set to universal quantum computation but are exponentially hard to simulate classically.7

This report presents an exhaustive architectural synthesis of the QMINIWASM quantum router, spanning the mathematical mapping of Clifford algebra to ternary logic, advanced compiler heuristics, the integration of Clipped Importance Sampling Policy Optimization (CISPO) and Cascade Reinforcement Learning (RL), and the operational protocols required to manage the non-Clifford boundary.

## **Pillar 1: Mathematical Mapping of Clifford Algebra to Ternary Logic**

The simulation of Clifford circuits classically relies on the stabilizer formalism, which tracks the evolution of a quantum state by tracking the Pauli operators that stabilize it.9 An ![][image3]\-qubit stabilizer state is uniquely defined by a set of ![][image3] commuting, independent generators from the Pauli group ![][image4]. Traditionally, this is implemented using the Aaronson-Gottesman CHP (CNOT-Hadamard-Phase) algorithm, which maintains a ![][image5] binary matrix tracking the presence of ![][image6] and ![][image7] operators, alongside a ![][image8]\-dimensional phase vector tracking the overall sign (![][image9]) of each generator.11

While the binary representation requires separate memory registers and distinct update logic for the Boolean presence of observables and their algebraic phase, the QMINIWASM architecture natively processes 1.58-bit ternary states ![][image1].1 This hardware affordance permits a novel, unified representation of the Pauli group that maps directly to ternary ALUs, bypassing floating-point arithmetic and bit-packing overhead entirely.

### **1.1 The Ternary Symplectic Pauli Frame**

Let the single-qubit Pauli group be ![][image10]. In traditional binary symplectic representations, a Pauli operator is encoded as a pair of bits ![][image11] such that the operator is proportional to ![][image12], with an external phase tracker resolving the signs and imaginary coefficients. QMINIWASM abandons this disparate tracking by embedding the Hermitian Pauli observables ![][image13] directly into a ternary coordinate system. We define the Ternary Symplectic Pauli Frame (TSPF), where a Pauli operator ![][image14] on ![][image3] qubits is represented by a ternary matrix over ![][image1].

The magnitude of the ternary element denotes the presence of the operator (![][image15] for absent, ![][image16] for present), and the sign of the non-zero element inherently embeds the phase of the operator. Furthermore, to capture the full global phase of a stabilizer generator (which can be ![][image17]), an auxiliary sign column is utilized. Specifically, for the ![][image18]\-th qubit in a given generator sequence, the mapping is defined by the coordinate pairs ![][image19]:

| Pauli Operator | Ternary X-component (vx​) | Ternary Z-component (vz​) | Algebraic Meaning |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **![][image20]** | **![][image15]** | **![][image15]** | Identity |
| ![][image21] | ![][image16] | ![][image15] | Positive X-basis observable |
| ![][image22] | ![][image17] | ![][image15] | Negative X-basis observable |
| ![][image23] | ![][image15] | ![][image16] | Positive Z-basis observable |
| ![][image24] | ![][image15] | ![][image17] | Negative Z-basis observable |
| ![][image25] | ![][image16] | ![][image16] | Positive Y-basis observable (![][image26]) |
| ![][image27] | ![][image17] | ![][image17] | Negative Y-basis observable (![][image28]) |

This representation eliminates the need for an independent phase bit vector for individual qubit tracking. The ![][image3] stabilizer generators and ![][image3] destabilizer generators are stored in a ![][image29] ternary matrix ![][image30] over ![][image1], where the final column dictates the global ![][image31] phase of the row.10 Because the Y operator is defined as ![][image32], the concurrent presence of ![][image6] and ![][image7] with matching signs natively encodes the algebraic structure of the Pauli Y observable within the ternary ALU.

### **1.2 Clifford Gate Update Rules in Ternary Logic**

The Clifford group ![][image33] is the normalizer of the Pauli group ![][image4], meaning that for any ![][image34] and ![][image35], the conjugation ![][image36] remains in ![][image4].12 In the QMINIWASM ternary WASM runtime, Clifford operations are enacted as linear transformations on the ternary matrix ![][image30]. Because the underlying hardware is optimized for BitNet-style 1.58-bit operations 1, the matrix updates must be formulated using only ternary addition, subtraction, and negation, avoiding modulo-2 Boolean XORs which would require casting to standard integer registers.

The efficiency of this approach lies in translating the conjugation rules of the Clifford generators into native ternary operations.

The ternary ALU handles this by detecting if both ![][image46] and ![][image47] are non-zero prior to the swap, and if so, multiplying the global phase column by ![][image17].

**Phase Gate (S):** The Phase gate maps ![][image48] and ![][image49].5 In the TSPF representation, mapping ![][image21] to ![][image25] requires updating the ![][image7] component based on the ![][image6] component, while carefully handling the phase accumulation. The ternary update rule for the ![][image50]\-gate on qubit ![][image18] relies on a specific ternary addition sequence. If this toggle results in an overflow (e.g., ![][image53], which falls outside the ![][image1] bounds), the ternary ALU wraps the value to ![][image15] and emits a phase-flip signal to the global row sign, perfectly mirroring the algebraic rule that ![][image54].

**Controlled-NOT Gate (CNOT):**

The CNOT gate with control ![][image55] and target ![][image56] propagates ![][image6] from control to target, and ![][image7] from target to control. The standard algebraic updates are ![][image57] and ![][image58].

### **1.3 Algorithmic Execution Framework**

By mapping the Gottesman-Knill updates to native 1.58-bit instructions, the QMINIWASM edge node processes stabilizer states with a memory footprint substantially smaller than a standard FP32 state-vector simulator, and significantly faster than a traditional Boolean CHP simulator reliant on bitwise shifts and standard ALU pipelines.

The algorithmic implementation of the ternary CNOT update within the WebAssembly environment leverages raw array manipulations optimized for discrete states. The pseudocode below demonstrates the implementation of the ![][image61] logic and phase wrapping mechanism:

C

// QMINIWASM Native Ternary Stabilizer Update: CNOT  
// Inputs: control\_idx (c), target\_idx (t), ternary\_tableau (T), num\_qubits (n)  
// T is a 2n x (2n+1) matrix with values strictly in {-1, 0, 1}

function apply\_CNOT\_ternary(c, t, T, n) {  
    int num\_generators \= 2 \* n;  
    int phase\_offset \= 2 \* n; // The final column stores the global sign

    for (int i \= 0; i \< num\_generators; i++) {  
        // X-propagation: target X \= control X \\otimes target X  
        int8\_t x\_c \= T\[i\]\[c\];           // Control X component  
        int8\_t x\_t \= T\[i\]\[t\];           // Target X component  
          
        // Ternary addition with algebraic phase wrapping  
        int8\_t new\_x\_t \= (x\_c \+ x\_t);  
        if (new\_x\_t \== 2 |

| new\_x\_t \== \-2) {  
            new\_x\_t \= 0; // X \\otimes X \= I  
            T\[i\]\[phase\_offset\] \= \-T\[i\]\[phase\_offset\]; // Phase flip upon Pauli collision  
        } else if (new\_x\_t \> 1) {  
            new\_x\_t \= 1;  
        } else if (new\_x\_t \< \-1) {  
            new\_x\_t \= \-1;  
        }  
        T\[i\]\[t\] \= new\_x\_t;

        // Z-propagation: control Z \= target Z \\otimes control Z  
        int z\_c\_idx \= c \+ n; // Z components are offset by n  
        int z\_t\_idx \= t \+ n;  
          
        int8\_t z\_c \= T\[i\]\[z\_c\_idx\];  
        int8\_t z\_t \= T\[i\]\[z\_t\_idx\];  
          
        int8\_t new\_z\_c \= (z\_c \+ z\_t);  
        if (new\_z\_c \== 2 |

| new\_z\_c \== \-2) {  
            new\_z\_c \= 0; // Z \\otimes Z \= I  
            T\[i\]\[phase\_offset\] \= \-T\[i\]\[phase\_offset\]; // Phase flip  
        } else if (new\_z\_c \> 1) {  
            new\_z\_c \= 1;  
        } else if (new\_z\_c \< \-1) {  
            new\_z\_c \= \-1;  
        }  
        T\[i\]\[z\_c\_idx\] \= new\_z\_c;  
    }  
}

This mathematical mapping explicitly proves that the entire stabilizer formalism can be absorbed into the inference mechanics of a 1.58-bit architecture.1 A tensor contraction in the LLM’s BitLinear layer can simultaneously compute classical neural network activations and evaluate Pauli frame updates for the quantum-assisted router. The absence of floating-point units during this stage reduces the thermal design power (TDP) required at the edge, unlocking extreme-scale local simulations.

## **Pillar 2: Compiler Heuristics and Quantum Routing Optimization**

While the ternary mapping enables ultra-fast, local classical simulation of Clifford operations, non-linear attention mechanisms in QMINIWASM demand universal quantum computation. This necessitates the introduction of non-Clifford gates, predominantly the T-gate (![][image66]) or the Toffoli gate.7 The Gottesman-Knill theorem cannot simulate T-gates without an exponential increase in computational resources, as each T-gate forces the classical simulator to branch into a superposition of distinct stabilizer states.8

Thus, non-Clifford elements must be physically executed on the remote QPU cluster. Offloading state to a QPU cluster incurs severe systemic penalties: high network transmission latency, QPU queueing time, and the physical noise associated with state preparation and measurement. Consequently, the QMINIWASM compiler must dynamically parse the hybrid quantum-classical computational graph and perform extreme T-count reduction and Clifford clustering.14

### **2.1 State-of-the-Art T-Count Reduction**

The optimization objective within the compiler relies heavily on phase polynomial extraction and ZX-calculus based rewriting.14 Modern heuristics, such as the T-count Optimization by Duplicate and Destroy (TODD) algorithm 16, partition a generic Clifford+T circuit into a leading Clifford network, a central non-Clifford phase polynomial network, and a trailing Clifford network.

For QMINIWASM, the routing compiler represents the quantum-assisted attention mechanism as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) ![][image67], where ![][image68] are quantum gates and ![][image69] are qubit state dependencies. The compiler algorithm applies continuous rewriting rules (e.g., spider fusion in ZX-calculus 17) to commute Clifford gates through T-gates wherever algebraically permissible. The goal is to maximize the density of Clifford gates in specific subgraphs ![][image70].

By isolating maximal Clifford subgraphs, the compiler creates large blocks of continuous execution that can be processed entirely locally by the ternary WASM runtime. The optimization problem is formalized as minimizing the T-depth (the number of sequential non-Clifford layers) rather than just the absolute T-count. Minimizing T-depth is paramount because it directly minimizes the number of synchronous network round-trips required between the edge node and the QPU cluster.14 If ten T-gates can be parallelized into a single depth layer, the edge node only incurs the network latency penalty once, rather than ten consecutive times.

### **2.2 Dynamic Graph Segmentation**

The structure of the quantum-assisted attention varies dynamically based on the input prompt length, linguistic entropy, and the dimensional demands of the BlochSphere projection. Therefore, static compilation is insufficient. QMINIWASM employs a dynamic, Reinforcement Learning-driven routing algorithm to segment the graph during inference.

The router must decide which attention heads are processed entirely locally (using Clifford-approximated linear projections) and which require full QPU offloading for non-linear feature extraction. To achieve this, the system evaluates the hybrid graph continuously. If a dense cluster of T-gates is detected, the router packages that specific tensor transformation for the QPU.

### **2.3 Cost Function Formulation**

To drive the routing logic, we formulate a parameterized cost-function compatible with Reinforcement Learning. The function artificially discounts the cost of Clifford operations to near-zero, while establishing an exponentially scaled penalty for non-Clifford gates.

Let an attention head computation be represented by a sub-circuit ![][image71]. The total execution cost ![][image72] is modeled as:

![][image73]  
Where the components are defined as follows:

| Function / Parameter | Description | Typical Scale / Impact |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **![][image74]** | Indicator function for Clifford gates (H, S, CNOT). | Drives local execution count. |
| ![][image75] | Indicator function for non-Clifford gates (T, CCZ). | Drives QPU execution count. |
| ![][image76] | Hardware cost multiplier for local ternary execution. | ![][image77] seconds per operation. |
| ![][image78] | Hardware cost multiplier for QPU physical execution. | ![][image79] seconds per operation. |

The objective of the dynamic router is to find a functionally equivalent circuit ![][image83] such that ![][image84] is minimized, subject to an allowable fidelity degradation ![][image85] in the attention output. If an attention head's weight matrix can be approximated by a purely Clifford unitary without the loss of semantic perplexity exceeding ![][image85], the router strips all T-gates, clustering the entire sub-circuit into a local WASM execution block.

This formulation inherently drives the system to synthesize "shallow-T" circuits. The router will prefer to trade a massive increase in local ternary operations (e.g., adding hundreds of Clifford gates) for the removal of a single QPU-bound T-gate. This cost asymmetry perfectly aligns the quantum compilation logic with the physical constraints of the QMINIWASM edge hardware.

## **Pillar 3: Integration with Cascade RL and CISPO**

Training an autonomous routing agent to reliably parse multi-dimensional tensors and select the optimal Clifford-approximation strategy involves optimizing over a highly non-differentiable, sparse reward landscape. Traditional Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and its derivatives often struggle in environments with sparse, high-magnitude penalty signals, frequently dropping rare but critical learning tokens during optimization.18 To overcome this, QMINIWASM utilizes Clipped Importance Sampling Policy Optimization (CISPO) 18 nested within a Cascade Reinforcement Learning framework.21

### **3.1 The CISPO Mechanism in Quantum Routing**

In the context of the QMINIWASM router, the sequence of "tokens" corresponds to the sequence of sequential gate scheduling and routing decisions (WASM vs. QPU). A decision to inject a T-gate and offload to the QPU incurs a massive latency penalty according to the cost function ![][image72]. However, this identical decision may yield a high reward by resolving a highly complex, non-linear linguistic pattern in the LLM's attention mechanism that a Clifford approximation would have failed to capture. Because QPU offload decisions are heavily penalized by default, the base policy naturally assigns them a very low baseline probability.

When the agent successfully identifies a scenario where a T-gate is absolutely mandatory for attention fidelity, the target policy's probability for that specific routing action spikes relative to the old policy. This results in an enormous importance sampling ratio:

![][image86]  
Standard Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) would clip the token update when ![][image87] exceeds the trust region and effectively discard this critical gradient. This phenomenon, known as gradient suppression, cripples the agent's ability to learn *when* to utilize the QPU, preventing the model from achieving high accuracy on complex reasoning tasks.20

CISPO directly solves this gradient suppression. The CISPO algorithm modifies the standard off-policy REINFORCE objective by clipping the importance sampling weights themselves, rather than clipping the per-token advantage surrogate 18:

![][image88]  
By clipping the ratio ![][image87] and wrapping it in a stop-gradient detach() operation, the clipped weight acts purely as a constant scalar coefficient.20 The gradient flows entirely through the ![][image89] term. This architectural adjustment ensures that every routing decision—especially the rare, highly penalizing but mathematically necessary T-gate injections—contributes to the policy update.18

The result is profound: the CISPO-trained agent converges rapidly on a highly nuanced policy that exhibits a stark, bimodal routing behavior. It aggressively projects states into the stabilizer polytope for ternary execution the vast majority of the time, but acts with surgical precision when allocating the rare non-Clifford queries to the QPU cluster.

| Algorithm Feature | Standard PPO / GRPO | QMINIWASM CISPO |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Clipping Target** | Surrogate objective function | Importance sampling weight ![][image87] |
| **Gradient Flow** | Halted for out-of-bound ratios | Preserved via ![][image90] term |
| **Rare Token Handling** | Frequently discarded | Retained, ensuring edge-case learning |
| **QPU Routing Impact** | Agent avoids QPU entirely (local minima) | Agent learns optimal, sparse QPU allocation |

### **3.2 Cascade RL and Stabilizer Polytope Projection**

To train this agent across the vast combinatorial space of potential quantum circuits, QMINIWASM utilizes Cascade RL.21 The training is staged across sequential domains, progressively increasing the complexity of the quantum-assisted attention mechanisms.

1. **Domain 1 (Pure Clifford Optimization):** The agent is trained on circuits containing only H, S, and CNOT gates. The environment strictly enforces the use of the local ternary ALUs, teaching the agent to maximize the efficiency of the 1.58-bit WASM allocation without any QPU access.  
2. **Domain 2 (T-Gate Penalization):** The agent is introduced to universal circuits containing T-gates. It must balance the CISPO reward for high-fidelity attention outputs against the latency penalties of QPU transmission.  
3. **Domain 3 (Hybrid Attention Integration):** The agent learns to route live LLM attention heads, optimizing for end-task linguistic perplexity across real-world datasets.

To prevent catastrophic forgetting across these stages, Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) is employed.21 The best performing checkpoint from Domain 1 acts as a continuous teacher for Domain 2, enforcing a persistent bias toward Clifford architectures. The distillation objective ensures that the final model retains its foundational capability to parse and cluster Clifford gates seamlessly, even as it learns the complexities of T-gate injection.

The theoretical mechanism ensuring the agent prefers projecting quantum states into the stabilizer polytope relies on the concept of Stabilizer Rényi Entropy (SRE). SRE is an information-theoretic metric quantifying the "non-stabilizerness" or "magic" of a quantum state.24 The reward function ![][image91] is shaped to include an SRE penalty:

![][image92]  
The RL agent inherently learns to evaluate the expected SRE of the attention head's target state. By seeking to maximize ![][image91], the policy ![][image93] learns to approximate high-SRE states with nearby vertices of the projected stabilizer polytope.26 If the trace distance between the target non-linear state and the nearest stabilizer vertex is below a calculated threshold ![][image85], the agent actively projects the state. This projection zeroes out the SRE penalty and triggers the local 1.58-bit ternary simulator, completely circumventing the physical QPU while maintaining acceptable accuracy in the attention mechanism.

## **Pillar 4: Handling the Non-Clifford Boundary (The "T-Gate Problem")**

Despite the extreme bias toward Clifford clustering enforced by the CISPO agent and the SRE reward penalties, universal quantum computation ultimately demands operations outside the normalizer of the Pauli group.28 When a non-Clifford operation is unavoidable to capture the complex, non-linear dependencies of a specific LLM attention head, the QMINIWASM edge node reaches a critical execution boundary.

Because the Gottesman-Knill theorem dictates that non-Clifford gates trigger an exponential superposition of stabilizer tableaus 8, the local 1.58-bit ternary simulator cannot directly process the T-gate without exhausting the edge node's memory via rank-decomposition.10 To overcome this fundamental limitation, QMINIWASM utilizes an advanced State Vector to Stabilizer Handoff Protocol 29, leveraging Magic State Injection 28 executed over the network.

### **4.1 The Edge-to-QPU Operational Protocol**

When the dynamic router commits a sub-circuit to the QPU, the edge node does not attempt to transmit a physical quantum state. Instead, it transmits the classical, ternary representation of the stabilizer state to the QPU, where physical execution takes over. The operational protocol functions through a precisely synchronized pause-and-resume mechanism.

**Step 1: Tableau Halting and Serialization** The WASM runtime executes the ternary CNOT, H, and S updates continuously. Upon parsing an unavoidable ![][image94]\-gate scheduled for logical qubit ![][image18], the WASM thread halts. The current ![][image29] ternary Symplectic Pauli Frame ![][image30] must be serialized into a highly compressed network payload. Because the data relies strictly on the discrete values ![][image1], 5 trits can be tightly packed into a single 8-bit byte (![][image95] states, fitting perfectly within the 256 states of a standard byte).31 This ultra-dense packing results in minimal network bandwidth overhead. The payload is transmitted to the remote physical QPU cluster.

**Step 2: Magic State Preparation and QPU Initialization** Upon receiving the serialized tableau ![][image30], the QPU cluster initializes a physical register of ![][image3] qubits into the specific stabilizer state dictated by the payload. Simultaneously, in a highly isolated, error-corrected factory region of the physical quantum chip, the QPU performs Magic State Distillation.28 The factory distills a highly purified magic state, typically ![][image96].

To apply the T-gate to the data qubit ![][image18] without decohering the rest of the physical state, the QPU utilizes a state injection circuit. The magic state ![][image97] is entangled with qubit ![][image18] using a physical CNOT gate, followed by a projective measurement of the magic state qubit in the Pauli Z basis.29

**Step 3: State Vector Handoff and Byproduct Correction** The outcome of the projective measurement determines the subsequent evolution of the state. If the measurement yields ![][image15], the T-gate has been successfully teleported onto qubit ![][image18]. If the measurement yields ![][image16], a byproduct ![][image50]\-gate (phase gate) error has occurred. This requires a Clifford ![][image50]\-gate correction to be dynamically applied to qubit ![][image18] to restore the intended state.28

Because the injection CNOT and the potential correction (![][image50]) are both strictly Clifford operations, they can be immediately absorbed back into a classical stabilizer representation. Once the non-Clifford phase has been physically injected, the QPU performs these final Clifford updates, effectively collapsing the state vector back into the stabilizer polytope, and reconstructs a new, updated Pauli Frame ![][image98].

**Step 4: Reintegration into the Ternary WASM Runtime**

The QPU serializes the newly updated ternary tableau ![][image98] back into the 5-trit byte-packed format and transmits the payload back to the edge node over the network.

The WASM runtime receives the payload, deserializes the 1.58-bit representations, overwrites its local matrix memory blocks, and resumes local, ultra-fast ternary execution of the subsequent Clifford gates in the circuit.

This state-vector-to-stabilizer handoff protocol 29 guarantees that the computationally intractable branching caused by non-Clifford operations is physically resolved by quantum interference on the remote QPU, while the edge device is burdened only with deterministic, low-power ternary data manipulation.

## **Bibliographic Context and Relevant Literature**

The architectural synthesis of QMINIWASM relies on a confluence of established literature across quantum compilation, reinforcement learning, and ternary logic. The foundations of 1.58-bit quantization are heavily derived from the BitNet b1.58 architectures, which proved that LLMs could maintain performance parity with FP16 models while restricting weights to the ternary set, fundamentally altering the memory wall constraints at the edge.1

Simultaneously, the classical simulation of quantum circuits is anchored by the Gottesman-Knill theorem and the subsequent Aaronson-Gottesman CHP (CNOT-Hadamard-Phase) algorithm, which demonstrated that stabilizer circuits can be tracked via a binary matrix in ![][image99] time.8 QMINIWASM adapts this into the Ternary Symplectic Pauli Frame, bridging the gap between quantum simulation theory and modern 1.58-bit hardware architectures.

In the domain of quantum compilation, T-count and T-depth optimization have been extensively researched, particularly through algorithms like TODD (T-count Optimization by Duplicate and Destroy) and phase polynomial synthesis.14 These works dictate the heuristic rules QMINIWASM utilizes to cluster Clifford operations. The routing logic governing these heuristics is driven by reinforcement learning techniques modeled on MiniMax's CISPO (Clipped Importance Sampling Policy Optimization) algorithm 18, which successfully mitigates gradient suppression for rare tokens. This is synthesized with the Cascade RL and Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD) frameworks proposed in recent literature 21, allowing the router to learn complex, multi-stage policies without catastrophic forgetting. Finally, the non-Clifford boundary execution is informed by magic state distillation protocols 28 and state-vector-to-stabilizer handoff simulations 29, enabling the seamless integration of physical QPUs and classical edge devices.

## **Conclusion**

The QMINIWASM architecture pioneers a vital symbiotic relationship between 1.58-bit ternary quantization and the Gottesman-Knill theorem, transforming the classical edge node into a highly parallelized, zero-multiplier simulator for quantum stabilizer states. By natively mapping the Pauli group updates onto ternary WebAssembly ALUs, the system bypasses the exponential memory and compute costs traditionally associated with floating-point quantum simulators. Furthermore, by employing a CISPO-driven Cascade RL compiler, the dynamic router learns an optimal policy that aggressively isolates Clifford subgraphs, heavily penalizes non-Clifford QPU network transmissions, and projects high-entropy attention heads into the stabilizer polytope wherever mathematically feasible. When universal quantum computation is strictly necessary, the state-vector handoff protocol smoothly delegates magic-state injection to a remote physical QPU, reintegrating the collapsed stabilizer state seamlessly back into the edge runtime. This synthesis provides a robust, highly scalable framework for deploying quantum-assisted, non-linear attention networks at the extreme computational edge.
